title: Anak Krakatau: Volcano eruption closes six Indonesian airports
description: Authorities have confirmed there is no tsunami warning linked to the recent activity of the volcano, which is in the Sunda Strait between the islands
body: Authorities have confirmed there is no tsunami warning linked to the recent activity of the volcano, which is in the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra.The health minister has urged residents in affected areas to stay indoors and wear face masks to protect against respiratory, eye, and skin risks.According to local newspaper Kompas, several schools cancelled activities on Saturday after students and residents reported eye irritations from the ash, while some fishermen had cancelled fishing trips at sea similarly reporting sore eyes.One resident, Aldi Candra Prayogi, told the outlet that he felt since Friday evening and it felt like "small grains of sand had gotten into my eyes", and that he needs to use eye drops to ease the irritation.The dust is so thick that he has to sweep the front yard of his house every five minutes, he also said.Anak Krakatau, which means Child of Krakatoa, has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa.The volcano - also known as Anak Krakatoa - collapsed in December 2018, triggering a huge tsunami which killed over 400 people, and displaced and injured thousands more on the nearby coastlines of Sumatra and Java.Scientists found that some of the chunks of rock that slid from the volcano when it collapsed were about 70-90m high.The Pacific Ring of Fire refers to a string of volcanoes, earthquake sites and tectonic plates around the Pacific. It spreads across 40,000km (25,000 miles) from the southern tip of South America all the way to New Zealand.Roughly 90% of all earthquakes occur along the area and the ring is dotted with 75% of all active volcanoes on Earth, that's 452 individual active volcanoes.

title: Diana memorial fountain shut all summer by technical fault
description: The Diana Memorial Fountain in Hyde Park - which has long been a popular place to cool down in hot weather - has been kept dry all summer due to a tec
body: The Diana Memorial Fountain in Hyde Park - which has long been a popular place to cool down in hot weather - has been kept dry all summer due to a technical fault.Royal Parks, the charity that maintains the central London park, apologised to visitors who found it without water "particularly given the prolonged high temperatures we've been experiencing". The fountain opened in 2004 in memory of Diana, Princess of Wales who died nearly seven years earlier. The closure was initially triggered by a mechanical breakdown in the pump that draws water from the local borehole. The pump was fixed, but software used to control the system then failed, preventing the water supply from being restored.The closure was publicly announced by Royal Parks on 1 July. The charity's spokesperson acknowledged that the fountain had "remained dry for longer than we hoped" while specialist teams worked to resolve the software issue.

schema.headline: Diana memorial fountain shut all summer by technical fault

title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' in foreign donor talks
description: Nigel Farage has said he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what ap
body: Nigel Farage has said he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what appears to have been a scheme to funnel foreign money to Reform UK.His former chief of staff Dan Jukes and ex-head of policy James Orr have both been removed from their jobs after an investigation recorded them talking about how to get money to the party from an American donor and asking a fake company to pay for polling.Jukes has denied doing anything wrong. Orr has told Sky News he will co-operate fully with Reform's internal investigation.In an interview with the BBC, the Reform leader said he was not listening to the discussion and revealed his family are "begging" him to leave his job amid increasing pressure.In a film by Verbatim Investigations and Channel 4 News, Farage and Jukes were present during a conversation in which it is suggested the US donor gives £500,000 to Reform through his UK-based son.Under electoral law, donors to UK political parties must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK, so cannot give money from abroad through a British resident.The proposed donation was never made as it was part of an undercover sting, but that it was seemingly entertained has sparked questions.When asked about the exchange by reporters at Reform's party conference on Friday, Farage said he was questioning whether the arrangement was above board. In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, he has now said: "I am not a compliance officer. I was in the middle of canvassing in the Clacton by-election. I turn up. I frankly wasn't even listening.""I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore," he said of the conversation in the Channel 4 film."The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have came from all over the world into a family office based in London. I know electoral law. I know donation law better than anybody."Frankly, the two individuals involved here have never been involved in fundraising before and they shouldn't have been involved directly in fundraising. They should have done basic checks and nobody, nobody should be brought to me, unless they've been vetted from."The row over the Channel 4 film has threatened to capsize Reform's conference, with Labour and the Liberal Democrats calling on the Metropolitan Police to investigate the claims. The force is assessing whether or not to investigate. Jukes and Orr - both senior figures in Farage's inner circle - have stood down pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation, but political opponents are demanding that Farage is investigated and takes accountability.Farage categorically denied that Reform had ever taken money from a foreign entity by channelling it through a UK donor.But as pressure ramps up on Farage in the latest crisis to rock Reform, he also told the BBC that "for the first time", he does not have his family's support to be in politics. "They would rather I packed it up and walked away," he said. He added he had not considered standing down, but "when you've got your family begging you to, it's not easy". Farage also condemned the hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters who descended on the Port of Dover on Saturday morning, causing major travel disruption.Farage said he "deplored" anyone wearing masks or balaclavas at public demonstrations. He added: "You should not be allowed to be masked up, balaclava-ed up and go out and protest on the streets of our country. It is wrong at every level. So I deplore what is happening in Dover today."Speaking after watching the interview, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said: "For a political party that don't like foreigners much they do seem to have a soft spot for foreign cash."We have rules in this country about how our democracy works and everyone has to stick to them."He added: "I think you see someone struggling to decide whether they're really serious about trying to run for power or want to keep the protest going."There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days". They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats. They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029. They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest. Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage. But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.   What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake. One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions". No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty". And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up – sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage". Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said. But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera – Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say." But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing. Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling – to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

schema.headline: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' in foreign donor talks

title: Is sleep tracking making your sleep worse?
description: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worseByBBC NewsSleep scores, magnesium, white noise machines - what was once the simple act of sleeping
body: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worseByBBC NewsSleep scores, magnesium, white noise machines - what was once the simple act of sleeping has become a minefield.Trying to optimise sleep in this way is called "sleepmaxxing". Take it too far, and you could end up with "orthosomnia" - the clinical term for an obsession with achieving perfect sleep.While it's not formally recognised as a condition in the UK, doctors tell the BBC they've noticed signs of orthosomnia in their patients, with some bringing their sleep tracker data into appointments convinced, wrongly, that they have a sleep disorder. That fixation is actually making people's sleep worse, they warn.So how and why did sleep become so complicated? And if sleepmaxxing isn't the answer, what is the elusive secret to a good night's sleep?'Sleep scores are completely made up'The first commercial fitness tracker to incorporate sleep analysis was the Fitbit Classic in 2009. Since then, many others - including Garmin, Whoop and Apple - have integrated sleep trackers into wrist-worn devices, as have smart rings such as Oura, Ultrahuman and RingConn.These devices vary, but in general they all provide users with a report of their night, broken down by sleep stages - time awake, light sleep, deep sleep, and REM (rapid eye movement). Many also give users a "sleep score".But the concept of a sleep score is "completely made up", according to Dr Alanna Hare, consultant of sleep medicine at the Royal Brompton Hospital in London."There's nothing recognised in sleep science that is a 'sleep score'," she tells the BBC. "That's just been created by manufacturers."Figure caption, How sleep-tracking can make your sleep worseHare says she's noticed trackers causing anxiety among her patients."I've noticed more patients coming to me with data from various trackers, with lots of questions about sleep that... is probably contributing to their sleep difficulties," she says.Even though some have had medical tests with reassuring results, this hasn't allayed their fears, she adds."It's great that there's more focus on sleep as part of wellness," she adds. "But sleep just does not respond well to attempts to perfect it."One proposed lawsuit against Oura, filed last month in San Francisco, alleges that Oura rings are unable to accurately measure sleep quality and sleep stages, and instead rely on AI-generated estimates that have "a coin flip's chance of being correct".In response, Oura told the BBC that it "stand[s] behind our science, research and accuracy claims"."We're committed to clearly communicating what Oura measures, what it estimates, and how members should use that information," the company added. Daytime impactStudies also show sleep trackers can affect how you function during the day, even if they're not accurate.In one study, external from the University of Oxford, participants were given sleep trackers which assigned them a sleep score. The scores were randomised, however, and had no relation to how the participants had actually slept.The next day participants rated their mood, fatigue levels and alertness, before tests checking their focus and reaction times.Researchers found that the people told they'd slept badly reported feeling more fatigued, and were less mentally alert - even though the sleep scores were all fake.'Cycle of worrying'This is something Jess Hill says she noticed in herself after getting a Garmin watch several years ago."I started to rely on the watch as my Bible for whether I slept well or not," the 32-year-old HR professional from London tells the BBC."I would think, 'I've had awful sleep so I'm going to really struggle today', even if I actually probably had okay sleep. If I'd slept really well, I'd be convinced I'd have to be on top - even though I was tired, I was pushing through things."Image source, Jess HillImage caption, Jess Hill was "obsessed" with her Garmin's sleep scores for about three yearsHer "obsession", as she describes it, with getting a high sleep score lasted three years, until earlier this year, when she started to notice the watch wasn't reflecting how she'd actually slept."I was awake the other week for four hours in the night, and my watch was like 'wow, great sleep!' - I literally was awake from 01:00 until 05:00," she says.The BBC has approached Garmin for comment.Image caption, Jess's sleep scores weren't matching how she actually feltDr Neil Stanley, sleep expert and author of the book How to Sleep Well, argues that gamifying sleep is creating more disordered sleeping."The thing with tracking your sleep is that it gives you a number, and this means you have a target," he tells the BBC. "So you get into this cycle of worrying about your quality of sleep or the quantity of sleep based on figures."He says he carried out research into actigraphy - wrist-worn sleep trackers - around 40 years ago. Though commercial trackers now are a bit more sophisticated, they work in much the same way - by measuring your movement - and have the same limitations, he says."If you want to measure sleep, you have to measure the brain," Stanley adds. "Unless you're measuring the brain's activities, you're not measuring sleep."So how can we actually sleep well?Hare recommends:Keeping your bedroom cool, dark and quiet - within reason. "That doesn't mean it needs to be pitch black, exactly 16C or totally silent," she says. "It should be coolish, darkish and quietish."Seeing bright light in the morning, which is good for regulating your circadian rhythm - that is, your body's natural clock.Doing light exercise, and eating a "healthy, Mediterranean-style diet with plenty of plant variability".Above all, keeping it simple - "anything else, you don't need it".

schema.headline: Is sleep tracking making your sleep worse?

title: Police slow to respond to Dover protest, says council boss
description: Police were slow to react to an "exceptionally well organised" protest that ground the Port of Dover to a halt for hours, a council boss has said.Kevi
body: Police were slow to react to an "exceptionally well organised" protest that ground the Port of Dover to a halt for hours, a council boss has said.Kevin Mills, who leads Dover District Council, told the BBC that demonstrators "caught several agencies on the hoof" when they arrived on Saturday.Hundreds of masked men chanting "stop the boats" blocked roads, causing miles of tailbacks and preventing access to the port.Kent Police is yet to comment, but cabinet minister Jonathan Reynolds said officers "did deal with it swiftly".Mills said the force "appeared to be quite slow to keep the roads and the networks open, which is disappointing"."The protesters knew what they were doing, I'm not sure the police did know what was going to happen," he told the BBC."But then I accept that the police resource is stretched."The Labour councillor said "no-one actually knew" what was happening on Saturday morning and there "needs to be a wash-up over that"."All in all it was a pretty traumatic day for a lot of people travelling, trying to get around their business," he said.Kent Police said on Saturday that officers made no arrests and described it as a "spontaneous protest".Mills added that the council later received complaints from villagers in Preston, where "protesters appear to have parked their vehicles before they came in".Chris Vinson, leader of the council's Conservative group, previously said the men had "loaded into rental vans" and then travelled to the town.Reynolds, speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, condemned the protest."Peaceful protest is an essential part of British life but that is not what we saw there with that kind of intimidatory behaviour," the business secretary said."I feel sorry for the people around Dover and the people disrupted by that."Police have not yet commented on who was behind the demonstration, which lasted from 07:00 BST to about 11:30.Anti-hate organisation Hope Not Hate claimed the Patriot Platform network arranged it, saying the group began meeting in July and had brought together members of anti-migrant groups from around the country.Demonstrators told the BBC they did not want to talk to the media, although one said "send them back" and another said "stop the boats" when approached on Saturday.Far-right activists Tommy Robinson and Danny Thomas both posted about it on X, praising those involved.Thomas wrote: "The experience on the ground today, was the overwhelming majority of the women and local people we spoke to were thankful that people were actually doing something."He praised protesters for showing "discipline" and said they had "stuck to the plan".Reynolds said that Robinson and others like him were "not interested in solving genuine problems this country has"."They want to exploit their online following and take money from the people willing to follow them online, and that's what that agenda is," he said."This government is about solving the problems that really make a difference to people's lives."Great Yarmouth MP and leader of Restore Britain, Rupert Lowe, said his party "proudly stands with those peacefully protesting against illegal immigration in Dover".In a video on X, he said wearing balaclavas was "undesirable" but "perfectly fair for people living in this Orwellian age".Follow BBC Kent on Facebook, external, on X, external, and on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Kent on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.

title: Majority Russian-speaking city in Ukraine considers language ban in the arts
description: Ukraine's third-biggest city Odesa will decide this week whether to back a controversial plan to ban the Russian language in the arts.The proposal bei
body: Ukraine's third-biggest city Odesa will decide this week whether to back a controversial plan to ban the Russian language in the arts.The proposal being considered by councillors in Odesa on the Black Sea coast aims to add to existing restrictions on Russian imposed by national legislation. It is particularly significant because Odesa is overwhelmingly Russian-speaking, although the ban would only affect public spaces and everyday usage of Russian would remain unaffected.For millions of Ukrainians, Russian is their first language including many of the troops defending the country in its war with Russia. But Ukrainian is the only state language and spoken by the majority, and some see Russian as a tool of Russian influence.The proposal in Odesa, which is targeted daily by Russian drone and missile strikes, calls for a complete halt to Russian-language content in music and literature, in streets, parks, public institutions and state-run arts and entertainment venues. It would also recommend a ban in privately owned spaces.In a city famous for Russian-language writers and musicians, it has provoked strong passions. The ban would extend in public spaces to old Odesa songs almost universally known throughout the former Soviet Union. All Russian-language books would be removed from display in public libraries. Currently, they can be shown, but not prominently."The Russian language is a weapon of Russia, and we need to try to fix that," says Odesa lawyer Artem Kartashov, who has advised local authorities on an official programme to "decolonise" the city of its historic Russian legacy."With Russian-speaking music and other things, Russians try to deconstruct Ukrainian identity and influence especially young people, because they grow up in a Russian-speaking environment."But comic actor Borys Barsky, one of Odesa's best-known entertainers, says: "Russian isn't [only] the language of Putin, it's the language of [writers like] Dostoyevsky and Bulgakov. "Who benefits from setting people against other people who love Ukraine just as deeply, only love it in a different language? Only Putin benefits from this."Russian President Vladimir Putin has often referred to what he falsely describes as  repression of the Russian-speaking minority in Ukraine as one of his justifications for launching his invasion of the country.Russian and Ukrainian are closely related, but distinct in many ways. Many in Ukraine speak a mixture of the two, known as surzhyk. Russian is the native language of President Volodymyr Zelensky, which he used often in his election campaign but has since used only Ukrainian in public.But a 2019 law requires use of Ukrainian in many public and professional contexts including education, public services and customer service.Public-facing workers - including waiters, shop assistants and doctors - must address customers or patients initially in Ukrainian, though they can later switch to Russian if the client prefers that.Odesa's Mask Theatre, run by Barsky, has been fined for infringements of the legislation including using Russian in publicity materials. A later inspection found further violations such as a cafe sign with the Russian word for coffee."This isn't even like Orwell or Kafka, it's just madness," he says.Public playing of songs by Russian citizens is already illegal across Ukraine, with exceptions for some artists who have publicly condemned the war, but Russian-language songs composed or performed by Ukrainians are still allowed.Under the proposals they would also be banned in public places.  Anna Nerush said it would not affect someone celebrating their birthday in Russian in a private room in a restaurant, as it could not be heard outside. "But on the streets, [hearing] the Russian language can be a real trigger, for example to [former] prisoners of war and people who've come from occupied territories," she said.Many native Russian-speakers in Ukraine have switched to Ukrainian in recent years, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. Photographer Natalia Mykhailenko switched even earlier. She has led tours of Odesa highlighting non-Russian elements of its history. These include landmarks such as a Cossack cemetery that dates back to before 1794. That is the year Russian empress Catherine the Great is said to have founded the city, although it has been widely questioned in recent years.A statue of Catherine was removed from a central Odesa square after a council vote in 2022, and streets have been renamed to commemorate some Ukrainian writers and activists."We must understand we were a colony," said Mykhailenko. "And these [language] laws are very important. I understand it's maybe sometimes not democratic. But without it, there will be no normal Ukraine in the future."Anthropologist Anastasia Piliavsky, part of a group called Ukrainian Cosmopolis which aims to defend freedom of thought and speech, believes Russian-speakers are being made to feel like second-class citizens who are deprived of their heritage."In Ukraine, the vast majority of people understand both Russian and Ukrainian. So the question is not really one of language, it's one of liberty," she said."Ukraine has been fighting for freedom. The point of this war is not to be under authoritarian rule. That's what Russia has to offer. So when fines, or the threat of being fired [for breaking language laws] arrives, then people start wondering: what are we fighting for?"It is unclear how much support the new language proposal has. It is opposed by an influential group of councillors linked to former mayor Hennadiy Trukhanov.Beyond Odesa, a national poll showed 80% support for Ukrainian dominating "all spheres of communication" in 2022. However, a more recent survey of students in Kyiv found that 82% chose to speak Russian during break times, even though Ukrainian is enforced in classrooms.One famous Odesan who found himself at the centre of the language controversy is Pavlo Viktor, a physics teacher whose online lessons have been followed by millions around the world. Ukrainian language campaigners criticised him for putting the videos out in Russian, his first language, although he later translated them into Ukrainian. He was later criticised for saying he would talk to scared children in Russian during missile attacks, if that was the language they preferred.Viktor is keen to take the heat out of the argument, explaining that currently about 10% of the Odesa population spoke Ukrainian in the street: "But if we wait 50 years, maybe 90% will speak Ukrainian.""Ukrainianisation must be polite and soft… not to persuade children to move from Russian to Ukrainian, but to make an atmosphere when they want to do this. It's the best way. And I hope that gradually we'll move in that direction."You can hear more about the language controversy in  Odesa in the Crossing Continents podcast Ukraine: Fighting Russia, Fighting Russian, available from Tuesday 8 September.

schema.headline: Majority Russian-speaking city in Ukraine considers language ban in the arts

title: Why more women carry the 'mental load' - and how couples can share it
description: Image source, Halfpoint ImagesByGrace Dean and Mallory Moench"My head's always full," says mum-of-three Stacie Matthias. "I go to sleep with a mental
body: Image source, Halfpoint ImagesByGrace Dean and Mallory Moench"My head's always full," says mum-of-three Stacie Matthias. "I go to sleep with a mental to-do list."She's talking about the concept of the "mental load" - the burden of planning, organising, remembering and anticipating tasks that keep a household running.These tasks include: remembering school trips, checking for updates in parents' WhatsApp groups, noticing which parts of the house need cleaning, monitoring how much sleep children get, scheduling doctors' appointments and buying school uniforms.According to academics, this is work that in heterosexual couples disproportionately falls to women - particularly mothers - alongside the bulk of physical household labour.All relationships and households are different, of course, but studies suggest clear patterns.Children in the UK have just gone back to school from the summer holidays, and Stacie, 37, from Stockport, says her mind often feels especially busy in September."It's that feeling of always having something to remember, organise or worry about that makes this time of year particularly full-on," she says.For Stacie this list of responsibilities leaves her mind feeling like a washing-up bowl that's being filled up throughout the day. "If someone's not helping you remove those pots and pans, your water's overflowing by the end of the day," she says, "and you're at tipping point."Image source, Stacie MatthiasImage caption, Stacie says she always has something to "remember, organise or worry about"In a survey looking into the mental load that involved 3,000 US parents, academics at the University of Bath and the University of Melbourne , externalfound that mothers handled 71% of household tasks that required mental effort, such as keeping track of when sheets and towels needed to be washed and remembering by when food in the fridge needed to be eaten.The study found that fathers handled many of the tasks researchers described as "episodic" - things that happen less often, such as remembering when to get the car serviced.University of Melbourne Prof Leah Ruppaner describes the mental load as being invisible, enduring and without boundaries. "You don't bring your dishes to work, but you bring the mental load everywhere," she says.The mental load is a popular topic on forums like Reddit and Mumsnet, where women seek advice about how to talk to their partners about the exhaustion of trying to juggle so many different responsibilities.Mums told BBC News they were often added to school WhatsApp groups - where parents discuss things like non-uniform days, school trips, birthdays and lost property - as the "default parent", while their partners never joined.Sophia, a 35-year-old mum of three in Portsmouth, pays for school trips and makes lunch orders on her children's school's app on her phone, but says her husband has never downloaded it.Sophia says she tried multiple times to explain the concept of the mental load to her husband - but feels he didn't understand and dismissed her concerns as "quick tasks"."They are quick tasks if you could just do the task," Sophia says, "but I have to plan for the task, I have to anticipate the task, I have to be 10 steps ahead all the time."Image source, Getty ImagesSam Berry, a deputy headteacher, content creator and married dad of two in London, says when his wife first raised the idea of mental load after his eldest was born, he "didn't really get it" and was "a bit defensive" because he thought he was doing a lot - changing nappies, feeding the baby and more.He would ask what he could do to help, but he says that still puts the burden on the other person to do the thinking.As Stacie explains: "I always say to my partner: 'If I have to ask you to do something, that's just adding to my mental load'."It took a few months of talking and listening for Sam to understand that it was not only about completing the task, but the thinking around it - not just cooking dinner, but what food was in the house, planning the meal, and doing the shopping.Clinical psychologist Natasha Wallace says some women come to her feeling stressed by the pressure they feel to organise their households."It's often, for them, not one enormous stressor," she says. "It's when they realise that they have hundreds of tiny demands on them and their brains and bodies just can't switch off."Many women are running on autopilot, she adds, so they often don't realise the extent of the cognitive load they're carrying, and this constant low-level stress can have an effect on the nervous system. In turn, this can cause poor sleep, irritability and decision fatigue, she says.Image source, Natasha WallaceImage caption, Wallace says being constantly stressed can impact mental health and restAnita Cleare, parenting expert and author of The Work/Parent Switch, said the overall cognitive drain spills over into our work lives and leads to unsustainable burnout.One piece of research found , externalthat men who earned more did less physical and cognitive labour related to the household, but that when women's earnings increase, they do less physical housework but still the same amount of cognitive labour.Women very seldomly feel it is a choice to opt out of family life, so the choice then becomes whether to decelerate their career, go part-time, or stop and stay home - with more and more women making that decision, Cleare says."If you lower the domestic load, if you lower the mental load, you will create energy, capacity, interest in being able to perform more and better at work."Why the disparity?Many of the women the BBC interviewed said they believed the disparity began with maternity leave.Wallace says that because women typically take much longer for maternity leave than dads do for paternity leave, they become the "default parent" very early on."If you become the person who knows everything, knows where everything is and has in the past done everything, everybody starts coming to you for everything," she says, "so you remain that central person even if you return to work."In the UK, mothers can take up to 52 weeks of statutory maternity leave, 39 of which can be paid, while fathers can take up to two weeks of leave with statutory paternity pay. Parents can also take shared parental leave.Some employers offer extra parental leave to their workers, but most people earn less when on maternity or paternity leave, which affects how much leave many fathers take.Cleare says workplaces can help by making examples of fathers taking paternity leave, not just offering it, and by setting expectations around when employees are contactable, and supporting career conversations for women.It can also come down to what are seen as traditional roles.Zach Watson, a married father of three and coach in the US on sharing the mental load, says his grandfather might never have cooked a meal in his married life, while his father did only a little.In the first five years of his marriage, his wife cooked most of the time. If he offered to cook, he would ask her what she wanted - a question that could actually add to her mental load.He learned he could come to her with options for dinner, having already looked in the fridge, and give her a default if she wanted to opt entirely out of decision-making. And if he needed help, instead of just asking "Where's the ketchup?", he could explain where he had already looked.Image source, Maskot/Getty ImagesImage caption, Women say it's crucial that their partners take full ownership of their tasksSam Berry says while some men do not care, a big group - his audience online - "actually are really good husbands, are really good dads, they are trying their best and want to do the best they can, but almost haven't seen it or don't have the language".Many women the BBC spoke to were keen for their partners to take ownership of certain tasks.Sam calls this taking on "a category of tasks" - so dad might handle all the school admin, while mum manages the food.However, he says equality is not necessarily about splitting everything 50/50 - because one partner might work more and another might like cooking - but about finding what works best for both partners.And if you traditionally hold more of the mental load, you might need to accept that your partner may do things very differently, and it might not always go smoothly, says Afua Williams, 40, a mother of two in London.Image source, Afua WilliamsImage caption, Afua Williams says she always has a lot to think about come SeptemberHow to lighten the loadThose who spoke to BBC News shared their own tips about how to manage the mental load equally:Communicate clearly with your partner about how you're feeling and the impact of your mental load. Zach calls it "labelling" - making the invisible cognitive and emotional labour visible. Don't have these conversations when you're feeling angry or overwhelmed, says Wallace, or it can feel like the other person is being "blamed or criticised""See what you can offload", says Ana Catalano Weeks, co-author of a study , externalon how mental load impacts work. Do you really need to organise physical birthday cards for your children's friends? Can you mute parents' WhatsApp groups and just focus on official school emails?Have regular check-ins with your partner - it could be daily, weekly, or seasonallyCreate a shared calendar so that everyone is aware of birthdays, school meetings and moreTake ownership of tasks from start to finish without the need to be reminded, Wallace saysDon't fall into the "efficiency trap" that the solution is just to be more organised, Cleare says. Remember that what matters most as a parent are moments of connection with your child - not eating certain vegetables - and that will help redefine expectations

schema.headline: Why more women carry the 'mental load' - and how couples can share it

title: James Bond: the 007 questions fans want answered about its future
description: Image source, WireImage/Corbis via Getty ImagesImage caption, The man who could be Bond? Jacob Elordi, Jack Lowden and Callum Turner are reportedly in
body: Image source, WireImage/Corbis via Getty ImagesImage caption, The man who could be Bond? Jacob Elordi, Jack Lowden and Callum Turner are reportedly in the runningByLizo MzimbaEntertainment correspondentJames Bond is special. Playing him propels an actor into an exceptionally elite group of performers. From Sean Connery to Daniel Craig, only six people have ever played him in the official film series.In the last decade alone the UK has had more prime ministers, and twice as many people have walked on the moon than have played the British secret agent.The last announcement of a new Bond was 21 years ago in 2005. So it's inevitable for Bond fans to want to have their questions answered about the future of one of cinema's most sought after roles, in one of cinema's biggest franchises.1. Who will be the next person to play 007?Image gallerySkip image galleryImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Paul Mescal enjoyed breakout success in the TV miniseries Normal People, and lept into the wider public consciousness as Lucius in Gladiator II and alongside Jessie Buckley as Will in HamnetSlide 1 of 11, Paul Mescal smiles while posing for a photo wearing a white tuxedo with black shirt and trousers against a grey background, in LA in March., Paul Mescal enjoyed breakout success in the TV miniseries Normal People, and lept into the wider public consciousness as Lucius in Gladiator II and alongside Jessie Buckley as Will in HamnetThis is, of course, the big question fans have been talking about for the last six years. And with an announcement edging closer and closer, the speculation has intensified recently.Many of the same well-known faces have been bandied about for months, if not years. Those names have generally included Henry Cavill, Harris Dickinson, Jacob Elordi, Jack Lowden, James Norton, Jack O'Connell, Callum Turner and Aaron Taylor-Johnson.More recently, other names have also been thrown into the mix. Earlier this year Variety reported that stage actor Tom Francis had auditioned, external for the role. And in late August Page Six claimed there will be more auditions this month, and that Gladiator 2 star Paul Mescal and Heartstopper and SAS: Rogue Heroes star Jack Barton are also on the audition list, external. The announcement about the next film's producers referred to keeping Bond's spirit alive "as he embarks on his next adventure", seemingly confirming that Bond would remain male. However, it's never been clear whether the rumoured names have been well-sourced inside information, or merely guesswork and speculation.2. Have the auditions started yet?Back in May, Amazon MGM Studios who now control the Bond franchise confirmed the casting process was under way, external. But little detail beyond that was given, the statement only saying: "While we don't plan to comment on specific details during the casting process, we're excited to share more news with 007 fans as soon as the time is right."It now seems that the right time is fast approaching. In an interview with Deadline, external  Amy Pascal, one of the next film's producers, was asked whether we might have news on who would be playing Bond by the end of the year. She replied: "I would say the end of the year is a good bet."Last month entertainment writer Daniel Richtman said, external on social media: "I hear they're in the final round of casting for James Bond and might have already found their guy."His post on X was followed up by journalist Jeff Sneider, external who said: "Heard the same rumour. First it was down to seven, then three. Now 'they may have found their guy'. Who knows at this point? But for some reason, I don't think it's any of the so-called frontrunners, including the Aussie…"The Aussie is almost certainly a reference to Euphoria and Wuthering Heights star Jacob Elordi, who was brought up in Brisbane and Melbourne before moving to the US to pursue his acting career.3. How do the auditions work?Image source, United Artists/EON/MGMImage caption, Sam Neill auditioned for Bond in 1986, but the role eventually went to Timothy DaltonThe audition process is likely to have been carried out in a similar way to previous castings. The scene that many would-be Bonds have traditionally had to peform is taken from From Russia With Love, where 007 comes out of his bathroom to find Tatiana Romanova in his bed. It's a scene where an actor relies on their physical presence, movement and charisma. No explosions fights or gadgets.As GoldenEye and Casino Royale director Martin Campbell explained to entertainment website Gold Derby, external: "The word is effortless. You never see Bond fumble, he is very economic, efficient and effortless. That scene covers all the bases, basically."And for a series where the stakes are so high, no expense is spared in ensuring that the film team know exactly how each auditionee will come across on screen. As the 007 team themselves have explained in the past, external: "Bond screen tests are elaborate affairs involving hair and make-up, costumes, sets, and other actors."4. How will the new Bond be announced?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Daniel Craig was announced as James Bond in 2005Generally, the unveiling of a new Bond has taken place at a London press conference in front of the world's media. But for the first time creative control of the franchise is in the hands of a studio like Amazon MGM. Amazon purchased MGM for $8.5bn in 2021, which included the rights to distribute James Bond. And they're reported to have paid at least $20m more for the rights to creatively control Bond's future.Having paid such eye-watering amounts, it seems more than possible that Amazon MGM might well wish to drive fans towards their streaming service, with any reveal of the new Bond being exclusively announced on Prime Video.It would almost certainly see a surge in streaming subscriptions. And such an announcement would still inevitably be covered by the world's press.Global James Bond Day on 5 October, the 64th anniversary of the release of the first film Dr No, is fast approaching. So this date might be a good day for fans to mark in their diaries for a possible announcement.5. What is known about the next film?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Most Bond film titles have been taken from the Ian Fleming storiesWe don't yet know what it will be called, or have a confirmed release date. Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight is currently writing the script, and Dune's Denis Villeneuve will direct. They and the team may well already have a title in mind. Or, of course, they may just be calling it Bond 26 for now.Most of the series have taken titles from the original Ian Fleming stories. Four of those remain unused - The Hildebrand Rarity, Risico, 007 in New York, and The Property of a Lady. Although elements from those stories have already been used in previous Bond films.Fans have also been busy putting forward their own suggestions for potential titles. Since the accession of King Charles III in 2022, those suggestions have included On His Majesty's Secret Service, and King & Country.As for a release date, it's been widely reported that the next film is likely to be released in 2028. That means it's almost certain that this will be the biggest ever gap between films, more than the six years and four months between 1989's Licence To Kill and 1995's GoldenEye.6. How far ahead are the Bond team planning?Only the Bond team themselves really know this. But Amazon MGM do have the financial resources to plan well ahead, and explore various issues, such as how Bond will operate over multiple films; will there be an overriding arc that will cover his journey over the next decade etc; will there be a film every two years, every three years, every four or five?Additionally, with such a huge investment, AmazonMGM will undoubtedly be keen to learn from  Disney's experiences with Star Wars, and Marvel's experiences with its Marvel Cinematic Universe, in how best to use the Bond franchise. While there might be appetite for multiple Bond spin-offs, eg Young Bond, the Miss Moneypenny adventures etc, they will also be wary that they don't over-saturate the market, and damage the films which are at the core of the Bond franchise.7. How will the next film deal with the ending of the last?The below contains spoilers for No Time To DieDaniel Craig's farewell at the end of No Time To Die saw him on the island lair of the film's villain, Rami Malek's Safin, as it was struck by a volley of air strikes, with the super spy apparently finally meeting his demise.Rumours have indicated that the next film might well reflect Bond's early years at the start of his MI6 career, in effect a reboot, which means that there won't be any pressure or sense of disappointment that the story won't reflect No Time To Die's conclusion.And in any case, Bond fans have been reassured by the message that has appeared at the end of almost every Bond film - "James Bond will return".It looks like soon we'll be finding out who that James Bond will be.

schema.headline: James Bond: the 007 questions fans want answered about its future

title: 'Not only did I survive, I thrived' - Meera Syal after assaults
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Dame Meera Syal's new memoir discusses her upbringing, motherhood and the challenges she encountered in her c
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Dame Meera Syal's new memoir discusses her upbringing, motherhood and the challenges she encountered in her careerByOprah FlashWest MidlandsDame Meera Syal has said she "almost gave up" her career after being sexually harassed and assaulted by two "predators" within the media industry."I was out of work, I was homeless, sleeping on people's floors, and then these two things happened in quite quick succession," the Wolverhampton-born star said in a candid interview with BBC Asian Network's Amber Haque.In her new memoir, Vigilauntie, which was published on Thursday, the actress shared that both incidents happened in her 20s, as she was struggling to secure a role.Now aged 65, she has opened up about the harrowing experiences and reflected on how she overcame them to become one of the most well-known faces on British TV.Image caption, Syal (left) in Goodness Gracious Me! with co-star Nina Wadia"It could have been a point where I gave up," she explained."It put some fire in my belly because the reason I wanted to tell these stories is that I did survive, and not only did I survive, I thrived."The anger of the injustice of the situation made me seek out a bunch of women that changed the course of my life."Syal described the first incident as "my first casting couch approach".She wrote that the man, a theatre director, insinuated he would give her a role in a pantomime if she engaged in sexual acts with him. She refused and was able to leave.Image caption, During a chat with BBC Asian Network, the star spoke openly about how the experience has shaped who she is todayHowever, a few weeks later an older male actor invited her to his home under the guise that he would help her progress with her career. Instead he assaulted her, she wrote in her book.The predatory actor has since died.The comedy star, known for shows including Goodness Gracious Me and The Kumars at No 42, did not report the incidents to the police and did not tell family or friends as it "was the culture" of the industry at the time.She recalled: "When I have talked about this incident to other women, particularly of my age, they've all said that happened to me and a lot of them have never talked about it because it was part of the culture."The 70s, 80s and 90s, it was absolutely part of the culture."You wouldn't even bother to report half of these things because A, you wouldn't be believed and B, everyone was doing it."Image caption, Syal also starred as in The Rising of the Moon episode of The Mrs Bradley Mysteries Rather than turning away from the industry, Syal said she found strength and support in women's groups and began helping others.The star added: "I got involved with Newham Asian Women's Project and Southall Black Sisters. I began campaigning because these issues became personal and I wanted to create South Asian women that roared."All of that came from the fury I felt at what had happened to me. It did change the course of my life."Syal was born in Wolverhampton in 1961 to Indian Punjabi parents, who had moved to the UK from New Delhi. She later attended Queen Mary's High School in Walsall.Last year, Syal was given a damehood in the King's New Year Honours for her services to literature, drama and charity.Image caption, One of her most famous roles was in The Kumars at No 42Joining the BBC in the 1990s, she rose to prominence as part of the team behind the broadcaster's sketch comedy, Goodness Gracious Me!In 1993, she wrote the screenplay for the comedy-drama film Bhaji On The Beach, and two years later she starred in the Channel 4 romantic comedy film, Beautiful Thing.The award-winner was a key writer and actress on the 1996 show, and later helped to bring Bollywood to the West End, by co-writing Andrew Lloyd Webber's Bombay Dreams in 2002.You can listen to the full interview with Dame Meera Syal on Asian Network Trending on BBC Sounds. If you've been affected by the issues in this story, help and support is available via the BBC Action Line.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Wolverhampton

schema.headline: 'Not only did I survive, I thrived' - Meera Syal after assaults

title: Russia-Ukraine war: US envoys begin Ukraine talks after Putin meeting
description: The envoys travelled to Kyiv by train after flying to Poland – Zelensky told the media that it was not possible for them to land their plane despite p
body: The envoys travelled to Kyiv by train after flying to Poland – Zelensky told the media that it was not possible for them to land their plane despite preparations.Putin and Zelensky agreed to halt strikes on each other's capitals for three days while the negotiators carry out their trip.While Witkoff and Kushner were in talks at the Kremlin on Saturday, Zelensky said he and his team were "ready for a substantive conversation".On Sunday, Zelensky wrote on social media that his country "has always been and will remain constructive". "We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer. Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed."A dignified character of the postwar peace is needed. Our proposals are ready," he said.Overnight, Russian and Ukrainian forces continued to exchange strikes, with Ukraine confirming they struck an oil refinery, an airfield, and two air defence systems.The country's defence ministry said they targeted the Ryazan oil refinery, which supplies the Russian army, and an airfield in Rostov-on-Don.Earlier, Ukraine's Air Force reported that Russia attacked Ukraine with 108 long-range drones and small cruise missiles.The country's air defences downed 82 drones and six missiles, but 11 locations were hit, with debris falling at a further seven sites. Saturday's talks in Moscow lasted three hours and were held behind closed doors in Putin's official residence in the heart of the Russian capital, according to Russian state media.Details are still emerging, but both sides have given broadly positive remarks without going into specifics.Putin adviser Yuri Ushakov described the talks as "constructive, extremely frank"."The talks were not limited to an exchange of views on resolving the Ukrainian crisis - economic issues and potential major, mutually beneficial Russian-American projects were discussed in considerable detail," he said.Ushakov also said "note was made of the Russian army's tangible advances in the combat zone" and that there was acknowledgement that talks needed to address "the root causes of the conflict".Despite an escalation of Russian missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities including Kyiv, Russian ground forces have made very slow advances for most of the conflict, incurring enormous casualties. Russia still controls about one-fifth of Ukrainian territory - areas that it seized back in 2022.The talks come after Russia and Ukraine have intensified aerial attacks in recent months.Ukraine says it has struggled to repel ballistic missile attacks due to a lack of interceptor missiles, while Kyiv has focused its strikes on Russian economic infrastructure targets, notably oil installations.

title: Why Munya Chawawa is 'jumping ship' from social media to Shakespeare
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Munya Chawawa says he is on "a conscious mission" to use his phone lessByIan YoungsCulture reporterComedian,
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Munya Chawawa says he is on "a conscious mission" to use his phone lessByIan YoungsCulture reporterComedian, content creator and documentary maker Munya Chawawa became a star in the "golden era" of online video, but says his stage acting debut in Shakespeare is part of a move to "jump ship" from social media.Recently, he has been immersing himself in footage of the UK's 1990s illegal rave scene.It was a time of hedonism and freedom surrounded by political and media panic - and is the setting for a modern take on Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, in which Chawawa will appear."I've obviously done a super-deep dive into rave culture and watched loads of rave footage from all these little free parties where they would find an empty field," he says.While some footage exists of those illicit outdoor parties, they came before everyone had phones and cameras - and Chawawa, 33, feels a pang of nostalgia for that age of analogue abandon."I absolutely miss an era where we were dancing for ourselves and not for a digital world somewhere," he says.Image source, Manuel HarlanImage caption, Munya Chawawa says he has taken rehearsals for A Midsummer Night's Dream "super seriously""We're all phone addicts," Chawawa continues. "The average person's picking up their phone 200 times a day. I'm on a bit of a conscious mission at the moment to reduce that."And interestingly, the top comments under all the videos I've been watching are people who were at those raves saying, 'I loved being able to dance, maybe get a little high, maybe get too sweaty for too long, and know there was no record of that.'"Chawawa was in his teens when social media and smartphones took off, and says he "took for granted" the brief time before any and every fun occasion was recorded and posted for posterity.If he ventures onto a dance floor now, he admits "my two-step has become a lot stiffer" out of anxiety that a wrong move could be filmed and send him viral."So yeah, I do definitely pine for those non-digital, in-person experiences, and I envy my parents for having them."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Chawawa taking a selfie with fans at the 2025 Brit AwardsThis is coming from someone who owes his fame to the digital age, after making his name with comic videos as characters like upper-class drill rapper Unknown P and chef Jonny Oliver.But Chawawa has since branched out from social media - making two Bafta-nominated TV documentaries, starring on Taskmaster and doing stand-up comedy."I've been making my short-form satirical videos for almost eight years now, creeping up to a decade," he says. "I have a certain skill set that I've acquired there. It's skyrocketed me to all the places I wanted to go."But I suppose the question at the beginning was always - if these sketches do work and they do catapult me into this new stratosphere of entertainment, where am I trying to land?"The aim, he says, was to land on "something bigger and onto a new challenge" - such as theatre acting.Image source, Manuel HarlanImage caption, A Midsummer Night's Dream will open in Chichester later this monthHe's starting by playing Bottom in Shakespeare's romantic caper A Midsummer Night's Dream at Chichester Festival Theatre in West Sussex.In this 90s version, his character is a member of the Young Conservatives and is "a very political Bottom", he says, while Theseus is a Tory MP who has shut down free raves in the county."I take it super seriously and I'm very studious when we're in the room," Chawawa explains of his preparations. "I'm taking notes. I'm learning all of these mad Shakespeare terms like couplets and quatrains and anacreontics and stuff that definitely sounds made up but isn't."And I think also it's the perfect time to maybe... jump ship, I think is the right word."Social media platforms and their algorithms have very much angled themselves against the creatives at the moment, I think."'Lost in a sea of content'He's not jumping ship from social media completely, but says the online battle for eyeballs has "turned into a little bit of a dogfight, where even good stuff, even really consciously thought-out material, is just instantly swiped to the bottom of people's pages".Chawawa thinks he was lucky to "enjoy the golden era of social media" before it became harder to cut through the noise."To be able to experiment, to be able to trial these characters and roll the dice on big ideas was fantastic because you were never getting lost in a sea of content."There's some mad statistic about there being tens of millions of videos uploaded a day now - but at the time it was like, 'I'm going to try this Jamie Oliver spoof or a Nigella [Lawson] character or the UK's first posh drill rapper, what do you think?' And it felt like the whole internet would give you feedback on that creative product."He adds: "I love the fact that social media has allowed me to have a career in stand-up, as a documentarian and now as an actor, so I don't have any sort of resentment to it and how it's changed."But what I will say is I was there as the sun was coming up on social media, and it was very fun."Image source, Faysal HassanImage caption, Chawawa set up the Black Boys Theatre Club, who have a debrief in Nando's after watching each playChawawa fell in love with the theatre when he went to see The Lion King when he was 16 and realised it was like "the best movie you've ever seen, but in real life".However, returning as an adult, he felt out of place as a black man. "In the shows I was going to, it didn't feel as though they were too welcoming to me being there, just through the small social cues."He had a lightbulb moment after watching For Black Boys Who Have Considered Suicide When the Hue Gets Too Heavy by Ryan Calais Cameron, which "I still think is the best play I've ever seen". Chawawa found himself thinking, "I wish every black boy in the world could watch this play."So he took a group of teenagers to watch it, which he describes as "the most fulfilling and magical and deeply moving experience".Inspired by their reactions, Chawawa set up the Black Boys Theatre Club to take groups every month to plays ranging from Dracula to One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest - followed by a post-show discussion in Nando's."Every time we go and see a play, it's not about the boys skipping out of it going, 'I want to be the next Billy Elliot'," he says. "It's more just them realising it's a safe space for you. It can be your home if you want it to be. You will thrive on stage or as an audience member, but just know that theatre is a part of your multiverse."Ticket pricesIn 2023, 10% of theatre audiences were from black, Asian or ethnically diverse backgrounds, according to Arts Council England data.Chawawa praises theatres for opening their doors to the Black Boys Theatre Club and other efforts to attract more diverse audiences, but says lower ticket prices and "a societal shift" will make a bigger difference. Next month, his club will travel to see him in A Midsummer Night's Dream - and he hopes more young minds will be captivated by the "snow globe of human emotion" that is live theatre."Really, truly, where else can I go in real life and watch somebody express all emotions without restraint? Sadness, anger, joy, envy. And I can be metres away, sometimes centimetres away from seeing real human emotion - not through a screen of any size, but in the room," he says."I believe that as more people do try and back off away from screens and digital experiences, theatre will experience a boom."A Midsummer Night's Dream is at at Chichester Festival Theatre from 18 September to 17 October.

schema.headline: Why Munya Chawawa is 'jumping ship' from social media to Shakespeare

title: Royal Navy aircraft carrier leaves Portsmouth for training mission
description: "We've returned from summer leave rested and ready for the next phase of our training," HMS Queen Elizabeth's commanding officer Capt Claire Thompson
body: "We've returned from summer leave rested and ready for the next phase of our training," HMS Queen Elizabeth's commanding officer Capt Claire Thompson said ahead of the departure."Sailing with an embarked battle staff, integration and training is essential whilst relearning the skills required to conduct safe and effective aviation as we ensure that we are prepared to deliver operational activity at the heart of Nato should it be required," she said.Capt Thompson added that the deployment was a "key milestone" for both the vessel's Nato role and its "journey back to the Royal Navy's 'very high readiness' aircraft carrier".HMS Queen Elizabeth is set to take the latter role on from its sister ship, HMS Prince of Wales, next year.Annie Hoare was among family members waving off HMS Queen Elizabeth from the shore, as her son Thomas is a Petty Officer Weapons Engineer on board.She said: "Watching a boat that big and knowing your son is part of this is absolutely an amazing feeling, we are all so proud."Her son has been in the Navy since 2018 and sent out on deployments in the past.Hoare admitted the "information blackouts" could be challenging but she praised the support the Navy provides for those who are missing their loved ones."The navy is amazing and really supports families and they have really turned my son into a fine young gentleman," she said.

schema.headline: Royal Navy aircraft carrier leaves Portsmouth for training mission
